title: Some scholastics confessed it beyond reason in this life, notably Cardinal Cajetan
source_text: III. Haec difficultas tam ardua visa est Scholasticis nonnullis, ut hac in parte suam ignorantiam ingenue fassi sunt, & existimaverint rem esse quae superat mentis humanae captum, quamdiu mortali hoc corpore gravatur. Quo de numero fuit Cardinalis Cajetanus inter Scholasticos vir admodum celebris. Is enim, quantumvis acutus & subtilis, hac in re nunquam sibi potuit satisfacere, & putavit concordiam liberi arbitrii cum divina providentia, in hac vita esse inexplicabilem & non intelligibilem, ut videre est in ejus commentariis in primam partem Thomae, quaest. 22. art. 4.
pass_a_gloss: III. This difficulty has seemed so arduous to some Scholastics, that in this part they candidly confessed their ignorance, and thought it a thing which surpasses the grasp of the human mind, as long as it is weighed down by this mortal body. Of which number was Cardinal Cajetan, a man very celebrated among the Scholastics. For he, however acute and subtle, could never satisfy himself in this matter, and thought the concord of free choice with divine providence to be inexplicable and not intelligible in this life, as may be seen in his commentaries on the first part of Thomas, quest. 22, art. 4.
pass_b_english: Some scholastics found this difficulty so hard that they frankly confessed their ignorance on this point. They judged it beyond the reach of the human mind so long as the mind is burdened with this mortal body.

One of them was Cardinal Cajetan, a very famous figure among the scholastics. Sharp and subtle as he was, he could never satisfy himself here. He held that the harmony of free choice with God's providence cannot be explained or understood in this life, as his commentary on the first part of Thomas, question 22, article 4, shows.

lemmas.gloss: as long as it is weighed down by this mortal body

choices.why: The faculty of free decision; 'free choice' is kept throughout, with 'freedom' for libertas.
